title: Alexa co-creator said AI singularity may never happen — here's why
excerpt: Alexa co-creator and startup CEO William Tunstall-Pedoe said an AI singularity is unlikely, but that if it had arrived, everyone would know.
content_html:
I'm a co-creator of Alexa and an AI expert. If AI singularity ever arrives, everyone will notice — here’s how.

As told to Agnes Applegate

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with William Tunstall-Pedoe, a 57-year-old founder and CEO who sold his voice recognition company Evi Technologies to Amazon in 2012, becoming a co-creator of Alexa.

Business Insider previously interviewed Tunstall-Pedoe about how Evi, an AI-powered search engine that answered spoken or typed questions, became an integral part of Amazon's Alexa. He told us his addiction to tech started in his high school and that early in his career, after graduating from Cambridge in 1991, he worked for Acorn Computers and the Isaac Newton Institute, where he did what he called "some more niche AI things." After leaving Amazon in 2016 to mentor founders and invest in AI startups, he launched UnlikelyAI, a neurosymbolic AI startup, in 2019.

Tunstall-Pedoe weighed in on OpenAI CEO Sam Altman's recent claim on the "Relentless" podcast that "we are now, like, in the singularity" — the point at which AI surpasses human intelligence and begins advancing faster than humans can predict or control.

This essay is part of Business Insider's coverage of expert responses to Altman's claim. It has been edited for length and clarity.

All sorts of friends of mine who aren't in technology have been reaching out to me over the last few weeks because they're suddenly having to wake up to what's happening at work or in their industry due to AI.

The number of people using LLM chatbots for all sorts of things is only growing, and people are becoming more aware of this change. Still, there are a lot of assumptions about AI singularity and what it means.

To me, the singularity is the idea that technology accelerates improvements in technology at an ever-faster rate. Eventually, it'll get to the point where the speed of technological change is so enormous and autonomous that the human race will get caught up in it and land in some magical future state.

AI is certainly continuing the trend of new technology accelerating old technology, but that's been happening for centuries, with the Industrial Revolution being a prime example. As we've seen in the past, it's not a new and novel idea for a machine to be better than humans at a task.

I think the idea of runaway AI, brilliant and perfect at everything and at a level of intelligence that's thousands of times ahead of what we see today, is implausible at the moment. I don't think we're in the singularity.

Machines have outperformed us in some tasks for decades

If you look at what the brain can do, there are things that computers have been able to do dramatically better than the brain for decades and decades.

If you think about math, people long ago stopped trying to compete with computers at math. If you think about memory, Google has perfectly learned hundreds of billions of webpages and can produce them on demand. Meanwhile, the human brain struggles to remember six or seven digits a lot of the time.

In some dimensions, LLMs are now superior to the human brain. They can talk competently on almost every academic subject, which no human being can do. They've learned competencies from large amounts of training data that cover a wide range of tasks and topics.

My point is, there are ways in which machines have been dramatically superior to the human brain for a long time; this isn't something brand new to worry about.

AI functions on human data

Part of the illusion of LLMs' extraordinary capabilities and why they appear so smart is that they've been trained on a meaningful percentage of everything that's ever been written; they've seen, read, and learned so much from training data.

But much of what we're seeing is based on the imitative capabilities that come from AI training on large amounts of data and a wide range of human actions. I don't think AI singularity is a natural continuation of that.

AI would need to show stronger evidence of what I call discovery intelligence: AI independently producing and evaluating genuinely valuable, paradigm-shifting ideas. LLMs can currently generate novel ideas, but they can't determine whether those ideas are realistically super valuable.

The singularity idea, to me, assumes that discovery-type intelligence is an extension of the learned-competence type of intelligence that AI already has.

Here's what I think we'd see if AI reached the singularity moment

If AI ever gets good enough to self-improve, actually innovate in AI, and it turns out there are no limits to its intelligence, then that would clearly be a very momentous point in time.

AI would then become extraordinarily capable very, very quickly because it will be able to keep improving itself in inventive ways. That rapid pace will be the singularity moment.

Generally, I think it's easy to critique the idea of the AI singularity because it kind of assumes reality is like a mathematical function and that intelligence is very linear. I think intelligence is a collection of things that you can do to various degrees of capability, so it's not clear to me that there is such a thing as runaway infinite intelligence, and I don't think true AI singularity level acceleration will happen.

We would recognize it if it were here

I don't think technology necessarily accelerates very smoothly. It accelerates for a bit, hits a wall, and then there's a decade or two before the next paradigm shift or the next big innovation unlocks further innovation.

I think even non-tech people would notice the difference between the rapid acceleration in adoption happening now and what would happen if the AI singularity ever comes. It would show up in pretty much everything.

content_html_zh:
我是 Alexa 的联合创始人，也是一名人工智能专家。 如果人工智能奇点到来，每个人都会注意到——具体方式如下。

正如 Agnes Applegate 所说，您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

这篇众所周知的文章基于与 William Tunstall-Pedoe 的对话，William Tunstall-Pedoe 是一位 5​​7 岁的创始人兼首席执行官，他于 2012 年将自己的语音识别公司 Evi Technologies 卖给了亚马逊，成为 Alexa 的联合创始人。

《商业内幕》此前采访了 Tunstall-Pedoe，了解 Evi（一款回答口头或打字问题的人工智能搜索引擎）如何成为亚马逊 Alexa 的组成部分。 他告诉我们，他对科技的痴迷始于高中，在他职业生涯的早期，1991 年从剑桥毕业后，他曾在 Acorn Computers 和艾萨克·牛顿研究所工作，在那里他做了他所谓的“一些更小众的人工智能事情”。 2016 年离开亚马逊，指导创始人并投资人工智能初创公司后，他于 2019 年推出了神经符号人工智能初创公司 BeyondlyAI。

Tunstall-Pedoe 评论了 OpenAI 首席执行官 Sam Altman 最近在“Relentless”播客中的说法，即“我们现在正处于奇点”——在这一点上，人工智能超越了人类智能，并开始以超出人类预测或控制的速度前进。

本文是《商业内幕》专家对奥特曼主张的回应报道的一部分。 为了篇幅和清晰度，对其进行了编辑。

在过去的几周里，我的各种非技术领域的朋友都在联系我，因为由于人工智能，他们突然不得不意识到工作或行业中正在发生的事情。

使用 LLM 聊天机器人来做各种事情的人数只增不减，人们也越来越意识到这种变化。 尽管如此，关于人工智能奇点及其含义仍有很多假设。

对我来说，奇点在于技术以前所未有的速度加速技术进步。 最终，技术变革的速度将如此巨大和自主，人类将陷入其中并进入某种神奇的未来状态。

人工智能无疑延续了新技术加速旧技术的趋势，但这种情况已经发生了几个世纪，工业革命就是一个很好的例子。 正如我们过去所看到的，机器在某项任务上比人类做得更好并不是一个新奇的想法。

我认为失控的人工智能的想法目前是难以置信的，它在一切方面都非常出色和完美，其智能水平比我们今天看到的要领先数千倍。 我不认为我们处于奇点。

几十年来，机器在某些任务上表现优于我们

如果你看看大脑能做什么，几十年来，计算机在某些事情上的表现比大脑要好得多。

如果你想想数学，人们很久以前就不再试图在数学上与计算机竞争。 如果你考虑一下内存，谷歌已经完美地学习了数千亿个网页，并且可以按需生成它们。 与此同时，人类的大脑很多时候很难记住六到七位数字。

在某些方面，法学硕士现在优于人脑。 他们几乎可以胜任地谈论每个学术主题，这是人类无法做到的。 他们从涵盖广泛任务和主题的大量培训数据中学习了能力。

我的观点是，长期以来，机器在很多方面都明显优于人脑。这并不是什么值得担心的新鲜事。

人工智能对人类数据的作用

人们对法学硕士的非凡能力以及他们显得如此聪明的部分幻想是，他们接受过对曾经写过的所有内容中有意义的百分比的培训；他们从训练数据中看到、阅读并学到了很多东西。

但我们所看到的大部分内容都是基于人工智能对大量数据和广泛人类行为进行训练的模仿能力。 我不认为人工智能奇点是其自然延续。

人工智能需要为我所说的发现智能提供更有力的证据：人工智能独立产生和评估真正有价值的、范式转变的想法。 法学硕士目前可以产生新颖的想法，但他们无法确定这些想法是否真的非常有价值。

对我来说，奇点的想法假设发现型智能是人工智能已有的学习能力型智能的延伸。

如果人工智能达到奇点时刻，我认为我们会看到以下情况

如果人工智能变得足够好，能够自我改进，真正在人工智能领域进行创新，并且事实证明它的智能没有限制，那么这显然将是一个非常重要的时间点。

然后，人工智能将非常非常快地变得非常有能力，因为它将能够以创造性的方式不断改进自己。 这种快速的步伐将成为奇点时刻。

一般来说，我认为批评人工智能奇点的想法很容易，因为它假设现实就像一个数学函数，并且智能是非常线性的。 我认为智能是你可以以不同程度的能力完成的事情的集合，所以我不清楚是否存在失控的无限智能这样的东西，而且我认为真正的人工智能奇点级加速不会发生。

如果它在这里我们会认出它

我认为技术不一定会加速得非常顺利。 它加速了一点，碰壁了，然后再过一两年，下一次范式转变或下一次重大创新就会释放进一步的创新。

我认为即使是非技术人员也会注意到现在采用率的快速加速与人工智能奇点到来时会发生的情况之间的差异。 它几乎会出现在一切事物中。
